entry.title: Where the Model Frequently Meets the Road: Combining Statistical, Formal, and Case Study Methods

link.title: Where the Model Frequently Meets the Road: Combining Statistical, Formal, and Case Study Methods

entry.content: This paper briefly analyzes the working or default assumptions researchers in the formal, statistical, and case study traditions typically hold regarding the sources of unexplained variance, parameter values, functional forms, time, and external validity. We argue that these working assumptions are often not essential to each method, and that these assumptions can be relaxed in ways that allow multimethod work to proceed. We then analyze the comparative advantages of different combinations of formal, statistical, and case study methods, and offer advice on how to combine these methods.

entry.title: Average Causal Effect Estimation in DAGs with Hidden Variables: Beyond Back-Door and Front-Door Criteria

link.title: Average Causal Effect Estimation in DAGs with Hidden Variables: Beyond Back-Door and Front-Door Criteria

entry.content: The identification theory for causal effects in directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) with hidden variables is well established, but methods for estimation and inference beyond the g-formula remain less developed. Previous studies have introduced influence-function-based estimators for broad classes of identifiable effects. When implemented through the observed-data density factorization, these estimators can require conditional density estimation and numerical integration, which can be statistically challenging and computationally demanding for continuous or multivariate variables. Prior work on related causal functionals has used sequential regressions and Bayes-rule representations of density ratios to avoid these requirements. Building on established identification and influence-function results, we make these reparameterizations explicit for effects identified under treatment primal fixability, Tian and Pearl’s necessary and sufficient condition for identification of post-intervention law, encompassing settings beyond classical back-door and front-door identification. We construct one-step estimators under alternative nuisance parameterizations and characterize how these choices affect robustness properties and nuisance-specific L2(P) product-rate conditions for asymptotic linearity and root-n consistency. The estimators accommodate data-adaptive machine learning for nuisance estimation. To address potential violations of the target parameter bounds by one-step estimators, we also develop targeted minimum loss-based estimators (TMLEs) that respect these bounds. Our robustness characterizations and sufficient rate conditions apply to both the one-step estimators and TMLEs. Building on prior efficiency theory for hidden-variable DAGs, we further develop modifications of our estimators that exploit ordinary independence restrictions. Implementations are provided in the R flexCausal package.

entry.title: The empirical discrete copula process

link.title: The empirical discrete copula process

entry.content: This paper develops a general inferential framework for discrete copulas on finite supports in any dimension. The copula of a multivariate discrete distribution is defined as Csiszar’s I-projection (i.e., the minimum-Kullback-Leibler divergence projection) of its joint probability array onto the polytope of uniform-margins probability arrays of the same size, and its empirical estimator is obtained by applying that same projection to the array of empirical frequencies observed on the sample. Under the assumption of random sampling, strong consistency and $\sqrt{n}$-asymptotic normality of the empirical copula array is established. The theory is illustrated by deriving the large-sample distribution of Yule’s concordance coefficient (the natural analogue of Spearman’s $\rho$ for bivariate discrete distributions) and by constructing a test for quasi-independence in multivariate contingency tables.

entry.title: Trajectory-based cycle-level pedestrian crash prediction at intersections: A novel non-linear link function for block maxima led Bayesian GEV framework addressing heterogeneous traffic conditions

link.title: Trajectory-based cycle-level pedestrian crash prediction at intersections: A novel non-linear link function for block maxima led Bayesian GEV framework addressing heterogeneous traffic conditions

entry.content: This study develops a cycle-level framework for estimating pedestrian crash risk at signalized intersections under heterogeneous, non-lane-based traffic. Existing approaches often assume linear relationships between covariates and parameters, oversimplifying the complex, non-monotonic interactions among motorized vehicles (MVs), non-motorized vehicles (NMVs), and pedestrians. To address this limitation, the framework introduces a non-linear link function within a Bayesian generalized extreme value (GEV) structure to capture how traffic effects vary. It applies extreme value theory through the block maxima approach using post-encroachment time as a surrogate safety measure, with each signal cycle serving as an analysis block. It also proposes a behaviour-normalized modified crash risk (MRC) metric to account for pedestrians’ habitual risk-taking behaviour in Dhaka’s mixed traffic. Seven hierarchical Bayesian models were estimated using Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulation and compared using the deviance information criterion. Models with a non-linear link function only in the GEV location parameter fit the data better than their linear counterparts. Results suggest pedestrian speed is negatively associated with crash risk, while flow and speed of MVs, pedestrian flow, and NMV conflicting speed show positive associations, though all remain uncertain. The selected model’s MRC estimate was close to the observed crashes at a 93% confidence level tuned to this dataset. These results suggest that the non-linear structure adds flexibility for capturing the non-stationary and non-linear nature of traffic extremes. This framework is a step towards proactive identification of pedestrian crash risk and after wider validation, it could support adaptive signal control and safety interventions in mixed-traffic environments.

entry.title: Hyperbolic inference for treatment comparisons relative to a preferred direction: An application to astigmatism axes

link.title: Hyperbolic inference for treatment comparisons relative to a preferred direction: An application to astigmatism axes

entry.content: The paper compares two independent von Mises populations relative to a known preferred direction. An angular Fisher information calibration represents each population as a point in a Poincar'{e} disk. A signed score at that point combines the population’s mean departure from the medically preferred direction with its concentration. We test equality of scores using separate likelihood fits and an empirical sandwich standard error. At every fixed pair of concentrations the centered statistic is asymptotically standard normal, including when either population is aligned with or opposed to the target. The resulting test and confidence interval concern the Busemann score difference. Simulations show that rejection under the score null can exceed the nominal level at the smallest sample size and is closer to nominal at larger sizes. Proposed method has larger empirical power for alternative with score contrast, compared to the existing one. An application compares the transformed postoperative astigmatism axes for the SNARE and irrigating VECTIS procedures. The estimated score is smaller for SNARE, but the confidence interval for the score difference includes zero.

entry.title: Efficient and Debiased Learning of Average Hazard Under Non-Proportional Hazards

link.title: Efficient and Debiased Learning of Average Hazard Under Non-Proportional Hazards

entry.content: The hazard ratio from the Cox proportional hazards model is a ubiquitous summary of treatment effect. However, when hazards are non-proportional, the hazard ratio can lose a stable causal interpretation and become study-dependent because it effectively averages time-varying effects with weights determined by follow-up and censoring. We consider the average hazard (AH) as an alternative causal estimand: a population-level person-time event rate that remains well-defined and interpretable without assuming proportional hazards. Although AH can be estimated nonparametrically and regression-style adjustments have been proposed, existing approaches do not provide a general framework for flexible, high-dimensional nuisance estimation with valid sqrt{n} inference. We address this gap by developing a semiparametric, doubly robust framework for covariate-adjusted AH. We establish pathwise differentiability of AH in the nonparametric model, derive its efficient influence function, and construct cross-fitted, debiased estimators that leverage machine learning for nuisance estimation while retaining asymptotically normal, sqrt{n}-consistent inference under mild product-rate conditions. Simulations demonstrate that the proposed estimator achieves small bias and near-nominal confidence-interval coverage across proportional and non-proportional hazards settings, including crossing-hazards regimes where Cox-based summaries can be unstable. We illustrate practical utility in comparative effectiveness research by comparing immunotherapy regimens for advanced melanoma using SEER-Medicare linked data.

entry.title: On min-Storey estimators for multiple testing and conformal novelty detection

link.title: On min-Storey estimators for multiple testing and conformal novelty detection

entry.content: In a multiple testing task, finding an appropriate estimator of the proportion $\pi_0$ of non-signal in the data to boost power of false discovery rate (FDR) controlling procedures is a long-standing research theme, sometimes referred to as ‘adaptive FDR control’. The interest in this theme has been reinforced in the recent years with conformal novelty detection, for which it turns out that similar tools can be used in combination with any ‘blackbox’ machine learning algorithm. Nevertheless, perhaps surprisingly, finding a solution for ‘adaptive FDR control’ that is optimal in a broad sense is still an open problem. This paper fills this gap by introducing new $\pi_0$-estimators, referred to as min-Storey (MS) and interval-min-Storey (IMS), which are built upon the so-called ‘Storey estimator’. Plugging these estimators in the adaptive Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure is shown to deliver FDR control both in the independent and conformal settings. In addition, these methods satisfy an optimal power property over any (regular) alternative distribution. The excellent behaviors of the new adaptive procedures are illustrated with numerical experiments both in the independent and conformal models for various distribution structures.

entry.title: A bivariate cure copula model with zero-inflated gamma frailty for right-censored data

link.title: A bivariate cure copula model with zero-inflated gamma frailty for right-censored data

entry.content: In biomedical studies, paired survival data arise naturally when two event times are observed within the same subject. Existing statistical models seldom accommodate both cure fractions and complex dependence structures. In this paper, we propose a novel bivariate cure frailty-copula model for paired survival data with a cure fraction. By incorporating a zero-inflated gamma frailty, the proposed framework simultaneously accommodates a cure fraction and continuous unobserved heterogeneity among uncured subjects. Dependence between cure statuses is modeled naturally via an odds-ratio parameter, while dependence between survival times conditional on frailty is captured through a copula. To provide interpretable measures of overall dependence in the presence of cure, we derive population-level rank correlation coefficients, namely tie-adjusted versions of Kendall’s tau and Spearman’s rho. For suitable choices of baseline marginal survival functions and copulas, the joint survival function admits a closed-form expression, enabling maximum likelihood estimation and likelihood ratio testing. Simulation studies demonstrate satisfactory finite-sample performance and favorable comparisons with existing bivariate cure models. In a real-data analysis, the proposed model is favored by information criteria. An R package, curecopula, implementing the proposed methods is publicly available on GitHub.

entry.title: Fast Training of Mixture-of-Experts for Time Series Forecasting via Expert Loss Integration

link.title: Fast Training of Mixture-of-Experts for Time Series Forecasting via Expert Loss Integration

entry.content: We propose a novel Mixture-of-Experts framework, referred to as Expert Loss Integration MoE (EliMoE), for time series forecasting. EliMoE addresses the optimization problem arising from small gating weights by incorporating expert-specific losses, which provide each expert with a direct learning signal independent of the gate-assigned weight. Specifically, the overall objective comprises the base forecasting loss and expert-specific losses, allowing individual expert prediction errors to directly influence parameter updates alongside the aggregate forecasting error. The framework also encourages different experts to learn from different temporal segments of the data. The proposed framework is further combined with a partial online learning strategy that enables efficient incremental updates of model parameters. By integrating expert-level loss information with partial online learning, EliMoE improves forecasting performance while retaining computational efficiency. Empirical results across five benchmark datasets from diverse application domains with different sampling frequencies show that the proposed approach generally outperforms state-of-the-art supervised neural forecasting models, including Transformer-based architectures such as PatchTST, as well as zero-shot time-series foundation models such as TimeMoE. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the expert-specific loss integration strategy, highlighting its contribution to enhancing predictive performance.

entry.title: Random weighting inference for linear regression under serial dependence of unknown form

link.title: Random weighting inference for linear regression under serial dependence of unknown form

entry.content: We construct confidence regions for a linear regression’s coefficients, with regressors and errors forming a stationary ergodic sequence of serial dependence not necessarily known. We weight the observations by random variables from an independent auxiliary sample and estimate the coefficients by weighted least squares. We prove the estimator to be asymptotically normal with the sandwich covariance if and only if the bandwidth shrinks fast enough for the weights’ randomness to dominate the score’s serial dependence. Wald regions have the nominal level, under short memory with the dependence left unspecified and under long memory with a non-normal least-squares limit. We derive a condition specific to the slopes and a bandwidth from consistent memory-order estimates, and identify the estimator asymptotically with least squares perturbed by independent noise. In simulations, we compare our regions with self-normalized, fixed-bandwidth, and resampled intervals under short and long memory, and we apply the method to daily wind speeds at Irish stations, a long-memory series.

entry.title: A Family of Quantile Functions Useful in Clinical Studies

link.title: A Family of Quantile Functions Useful in Clinical Studies

entry.content: Motivated by upper-tail quantile-domain summaries, we study the quantile-based effectiveness persistence function defined as the ratio between the tail mean and the quantile function. We derive statistical properties of this measure and consider a rational (M"obius) specification of the quantile-based effectiveness persistence function. Under natural boundary conditions, this specification reduces to a canonical form, in which remaining life relative to elapsed time is proportional to the survival odds. The resulting canonical family defines a two-parameter class of non-negative distributions through its quantile function. Various properties, including descriptive measures, L-moments, and quantile-based reliability concepts, are derived for this class. Estimation of the model parameters using maximum likelihood is also developed. The proposed family is illustrated using a real survival dataset.

entry.title: A Deep Zero-Inflated Model of North Atlantic Right Whale Presence To Support Blue Economy Management

link.title: A Deep Zero-Inflated Model of North Atlantic Right Whale Presence To Support Blue Economy Management

entry.content: Effective modeling of endangered marine mammal species, such as the North Atlantic Right Whale, is critical for balancing marine conservation with the growing blue economy. Passive acoustic monitoring data collected by autonomous underwater vehicles provide new opportunities for localized marine species detection and oceanographic sensing, but introduce complex statistical challenges such as zero inflation, imperfect detection, and intricate dependence structures. In response, we propose the Deep Zero-Inflated Bernoulli (DeepZIB) model, a deep statistical method which jointly models latent species presence and conditional detection probabilities while learning complex habitat relationships from heterogeneous covariate information. We establish theoretical results on the model’s structural properties and conduct simulation experiments to demonstrate its ability to recover underlying parameters and latent presence fields. Application to real-world passive acoustic monitoring data on the North Atlantic Right Whale along the U.S. East Coast demonstrates improved model adequacy and predictive performance in capturing the species’ dynamic and spatially varying habitat. We demonstrate DeepZIB’s ability to generate high-resolution, spatially and temporally varying presence maps, providing valuable insights for targeted and risk-aware management of blue economy industries, ranging from offshore and marine energy, to fisheries management and maritime transport

entry.title: Towards Fair Comparisons of AI- and Physics-Based Weather Models for Extreme Events via the Weighted Potential CRPS

link.title: Towards Fair Comparisons of AI- and Physics-Based Weather Models for Extreme Events via the Weighted Potential CRPS

entry.content: We study whether deterministic AI weather prediction (AIWP) models issue more informative forecasts for extreme weather events than deterministic numerical weather prediction (NWP) models. The deterministic model output is subjected to statistical post-processing via isotonic distributional regression (IDR), or EasyUQ, before the resulting probabilistic forecasts are assessed using weighted versions of the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS). This extends the recently proposed Potential CRPS (PCRPS) measure to focus on extreme outcomes. Since IDR exhibits optimality properties with respect to weighted versions of the CRPS, the proposed approach inherits desirable properties of the PCRPS, and, in particular, facilitates fair comparisons between data-driven and physics-based models when forecasting extreme weather events. We apply this evaluation framework to forecasts in the WeatherBench 2 dataset issued by the AIWP models GraphCast, Pangu-Weather, and FuXi, with the ECMWF’s high-resolution NWP model serving as a physics-based reference. The forecast models are compared when predicting mean sea level pressure, temperature, wind speed, and precipitation extremes, defined as exceedances or non-exceedances of thresholds obtained from historical observation data. Across a range of extreme-event thresholds, including thresholds corresponding to record-breaking events, the ranking of the forecast models remains largely unchanged. We find that AIWP models, particularly GraphCast and FuXi, result in the most informative forecasts for extreme weather events across most settings, suggesting that AIWP models have the potential to outperform NWP models when forecasting extremes.

entry.title: Inverse Probability Weighting in a Post-Bayesian World

link.title: Inverse Probability Weighting in a Post-Bayesian World

entry.content: We present a rationale for the use of Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW) in a post-Bayesian framework, in which the bias-correction provided by IPW in a frequentist context is reframed as a retargetting of the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the statistical model and the true data-generating process. We provide a coherent argument in support of this approach, including theoretical results concerning convergence and properties of the generalised belief posteriors. We present examples demonstrating the utility of post-Bayesian IPW in practice: these include two simulated examples of inference under selection bias in the observed data, and a large-scale real-data example concerning systematic biases present in registry data when using prostate-specific antigen (PSA) to predict prostate cancer mortality. The empirical and theoretical results together show the utility of IPW to address classes of problems previously intractable within a principled Bayesian approach.

link.title: Transferring supremum-norm rates and weak convergence of covariance kernel estimators to functional principal components

entry.content: We show that $L_2$-perturbation theory can be used to transfer rates of convergence in the supremum norm as well as weak convergence in the space of continuous functions from covariance kernel estimators to the associated functional \rev{principal} components. We also present results of numerical experiments in which we use the Nystr"om method to compute functional principal components and eigenvalues, and give an empirical illustration to series of daily temperature curves.

entry.title: Randomization Tests in Randomized Saturation Designs

link.title: Randomization Tests in Randomized Saturation Designs

entry.content: Randomized saturation designs are widely used to study spillover effects in clustered populations. In these designs, clusters are first assigned to treatment saturation levels, and units are then randomized within clusters according to the assigned saturation. We first compare each unit’s untreated potential outcomes at two saturation levels: the partially sharp null requires zero spillover for every unit, while the bounded null imposes a prespecified upper bound on each unit’s spillover effect. entry.title: Fitting the topology of synthetic particle systems with a novel graph representation

link.title: Fitting the topology of synthetic particle systems with a novel graph representation

entry.content: The shape and arrangement of particles in a material determine its macroscopic properties. The generation of synthetic data with varying particle structure, often represented as 3D voxel images, combined with simulation of macroscopic properties reveals structure-property relations. Most particle generation models focus on single-particle characteristics like shape and size. We aim at fitting the topology of the particle system using tools from persistent homology. However, the large size of the required 3D image data makes existing methods computationally infeasible. We bridge this gap by introducing a novel graph representation of particle systems and transferring the computation of persistent homology from the image domain to the graph domain. This yields a postprocessing method for synthetic images of particle systems, that is independent of the underlying generation method and improves topological and geometrical agreement with real particle systems while preserving morphological characteristics such as the particle size distribution.

entry.title: Forecast combination under temporal constraints: An application to day-ahead electricity prices

link.title: Forecast combination under temporal constraints: An application to day-ahead electricity prices

entry.content: Day-ahead electricity prices are forecast by many competing models and at several temporal granularities, from hourly prices to block and baseload products. The resulting forecasts suffer from two distinct problems: forecasts produced at different granularities are incoherent, as the aggregates do not match the averages of their components, and no single model is the most accurate in every market, period and level. We address both problems in one step by applying the coherent forecast combination framework, recently proposed for linearly constrained multiple time series, to temporal hierarchies. The resulting temporal coherent combination pools the forecasts that the competing experts produce at all the levels of the hierarchy into a single forecast that satisfies the aggregation constraints and has minimum error variance among the linear unbiased combinations. Since the optimal solution depends on a high-dimensional error covariance matrix, we compare different estimators obtained by crossing correlation structures with linear and nonlinear shrinkage approaches, and we contrast the simultaneous solution with sequential strategies. Using the base forecasts of four model classes for the German and Spanish day-ahead markets, the combined forecasts significantly outperform the base forecasts at every temporal level and are never significantly less accurate than the best reconciled expert, often improving upon it significantly.

entry.title: Augmented Inverse Hybrid Weighting: Robust Inference under Deterministic and Random Distribution Shifts

link.title: Augmented Inverse Hybrid Weighting: Robust Inference under Deterministic and Random Distribution Shifts

entry.content: Reweighting source samples to match a target covariate distribution is a standard response to distribution shift when generalizing evidence across populations. It is well suited to deterministic, learnable covariate discrepancies, but can fail when source–target differences extend beyond covariate shift or when estimation of the density-ratio weights is unstable. We introduce a new model where the discrepancy between two population laws comprises a deterministic covariate shift and a non-systematic component, modeled as random perturbation of the probability space. This separates systematic shifts, treated as bias and corrected by reweighting, from random perturbations, treated as distributional uncertainty and reduced by dataset pooling. Under pure random perturbations, this principle yields Augmented Inverse Distance Weighting, which combines regression augmentation with variance-optimal dataset-level pooling and attains asymptotic variance no larger than exact covariate balancing. When both components are present, we develop Augmented Inverse Hybrid Weighting, which interpolates between AIDW and standard augmented importance weighting. Both estimators tradeoff sampling and distributional uncertainty via a distributional distance quantifying the strength of random perturbations. We establish asymptotic normality of both estimators and provide tuning and diagnostic tools. On three real-world multi-site datasets exhibiting diverse distribution shifts, the proposed methods consistently reduce mean-squared error compared with weighting baselines, and improve empirical coverage when covariate-shift adjustment alone undercovers.

entry.title: COMPACT: Spectral Adjustment Scores from an Exhaustive and Nonredundant Set of Invariant Relations

link.title: COMPACT: Spectral Adjustment Scores from an Exhaustive and Nonredundant Set of Invariant Relations

entry.content: Observational datasets frequently contain many baseline variables, yet investigators estimating causal effects may not know which variables to include in the adjustment set. Confounding information may also be distributed weakly across many variables. Propensity scores can simplify adjustment by reducing high-dimensional covariates to a scalar with binary treatment. Although the propensity score is the coarsest balancing score, this balancing property does not necessarily distinguish among causal structures relevant to adjustment. We instead examine all causal graphs among a candidate score, treatment, and outcome while allowing latent variables. Under faithfulness, we identify all unconditional and conditional dependence relations that remain unchanged when the treatment-to-outcome edge is added or removed, leaving treatment-effect estimation to the downstream analysis. Together, these relations define the smallest compatible graph class expressible through the relations considered. We then develop the proposed algorithm, which implements this criterion through a generalized eigenvalue problem whose score space targets the span of a treatment-balancing coordinate and a residual-outcome coordinate. We show that sufficiently informative proxies can recover this span without direct observation of the adjustment variables, characterize the resulting score-recovery and downstream causal-estimation errors, and establish bootstrap validity for the full procedure. Simulations and a real-data application demonstrate superior performance over several alternatives.

entry.title: Estimating Global Network Density from Snowball Samples

link.title: Estimating Global Network Density from Snowball Samples

entry.content: Many analyses aim to estimate a global property of a population network, such as its density, yet only a subsample of the network is observed. Ignoring the sampling scheme, and treating the samples as complete networks leads to biased inference. Although this selection problem is generally intractable, we show that it admits an exact solution for snowball samples drawn from Erd\H{o}s–R'enyi networks. We derive the exact likelihood of such a sample, showing that it forms a curved exponential family in the edge probability with a low-dimensional sufficient statistic. We obtain the maximum likelihood estimator that accounts for the sampling design, alongside valid confidence intervals constructed by inverting a test based on the exact sampling distribution, via Monte Carlo simulation. Simulations show that this estimator remains unbiased even when observing as little as 0.1\% of the vertices, with nominal confidence interval coverage. We further assess robustness to departures from the Erd\H{o}s–R'enyi assumption using scale-free and small-world synthetic networks, as well as a real Facebook ego network. We find that, while the corrected estimator no longer attains unbiasedness under these departures, it still substantially outperforms the naive alternative throughout.

entry.title: Bessel-Debiased Pseudo-Marginal MCMC for Generalised Bayesian Inference

link.title: Bessel-Debiased Pseudo-Marginal MCMC for Generalised Bayesian Inference

entry.content: Generalised Bayesian inference exponentiates a weighted loss, sometimes an integral estimated by simulation. Loss estimators generally give biased posterior weights which Pseudo-Marginal MCMC does not correct, and greater variability raises computational cost. We introduce Sign-Corrected Bessel Debiasing (SCBD), a signed pseudo-marginal method using independent block estimates from ordinary Monte Carlo or randomised quasi-Monte Carlo (RQMC). The correction is exact for i.i.d. Gaussian block estimates with unknown variance. For non-Gaussian blocks, we bound the posterior error in total variation. Under regularity conditions, the correction improves the fixed-data Monte Carlo bound from $O(M_n^{-1})$ to $O(M_n^{-2})$, where $M_n$ counts loss-integrand evaluations per loss estimate. Suppose the RQMC variance for a block of size $B$ is uniformly $O(B^{-\alpha}(\log B)^{d-1})$ in fixed dimension $d$. With a fixed number of blocks and a learning rate proportional to the sample size $n$, a per-proposal budget of order $n^{2/\alpha}$, up to logarithmic factors, suffices to keep the leading log-weight variance bounded. Our examples show that favourable RQMC representations can inherit this budget scaling and that RQMC variance reduction complements Bessel correction. Once the block estimates have been formed, the Bessel correction comes at negligible additional cost. The correction is generic, straightforward to implement, and supported by theory.

entry.title: From priors to performance: enhancing statistical efficiency with Bayesian dynamic borrowing

link.title: From priors to performance: enhancing statistical efficiency with Bayesian dynamic borrowing

entry.content: One of the main advantages of the Bayesian approach to statistical inference is the flexibility in incorporating information from various sources, from expert opinion to historical data. Whereas the literature on Bayesian dynamic borrowing is rich, practical guidance for how to implement such methods is comparatively sparse. We thoroughly review the most common dynamic borrowing approaches for external data, including how to incorporate multiple historical data sets. We then show how these techniques can be used in practice, using publicly available software, to perform important statistical tasks such as model selection, average treatment effect estimation and prior sensitivity analysis. The aim is to make analysts more confident in their use of Bayesian methods to incorporate external data. All code is made publicly available in a companion GitHub repository (https://github.com/EzequielEBS/hdbayes-tutorial).

entry.title: Multiple Testing Of Composite Null Hypotheses With High Dimensional Count Data: A Local False Discovery Rate Approach

link.title: Multiple Testing Of Composite Null Hypotheses With High Dimensional Count Data: A Local False Discovery Rate Approach

entry.content: High throughput sequencing technology is routinely used to generate high dimensional (HD) count data. One objective is to determine which variables are associated with a covariate via the testing of multiple null hypotheses, say $H_m:\beta_m = 0$ for $m = 1, 2, …, M$ where each $\beta_m$ is a regression parameter. The standard approach computes a $p$-value for each null hypothesis and applies some false discovery rate (FDR) method to determine which null hypotheses are rejected, i.e. which variables can be discovered as associated with the covariate. However, even if data are well modeled'', this approach tends to provide a misleading list of discoveries in that someuninteresting’’ negligible associations ($\beta_m \approx 0$) are discovered, while other interesting associations are not. This paper formally addresses this issue using Poisson Mixture models and a Local FDR (PMLFDR) procedure for testing of multiple composite null hypotheses $H_m:\beta_m\in[-\epsilon,\epsilon]$. It is shown that PMLFDR procedures allow for consistently estimable expressions for overdispersion, provide asymptotically optimal FDR control, and are robust with respect to model misspecification. Simulation studies and real data analysis illustrate that PMLFDR procedures perform favorably compared to established procedures in that they a) are flexible enough to model most HD count data regardless of the technology used in generation b) allow for continuous and categorical covariates and c) yield more meaningful discoveries without sacrificing FDR control.

entry.title: A Bayesian Distance-Weighted Ising Model for Task-Related Regional Analysis of Neuroimaging Data

link.title: A Bayesian Distance-Weighted Ising Model for Task-Related Regional Analysis of Neuroimaging Data

entry.content: Neuroimaging analysis commonly involves identifying task-relevant brain regions and examining functional connectivity. These objectives are typically addressed separately, without a model-based framework. We propose a Bayesian distance-weighted Ising model that jointly quantifies regional importance for task-label prediction and functional connectivity between brain regions. The Ising model favors agreement between interacting labels. We extend it with region-specific interaction parameters and weights based on distances between functional signals. The parameters quantify regional importance for distinguishing tasks, while the weights measure functional connectivity through signal similarity between regions. Inference for this model is challenging because the signals may be observed on unequal time grids and the likelihood function contains an intractable normalizing constant. To address this, we use a basis expansion and an auxiliary variable Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm. We apply the method to functional near-infrared spectroscopy data from younger and older adults, comparing resting-state and task-related activity. The model reveals age-dependent patterns of regional importance and connectivity. Among younger adults, the left orbitofrontal cortex contributes more strongly to task discrimination than the dorsolateral prefrontal and frontopolar cortices, whereas regional differences are less evident among older adults. Older adults also exhibit greater bilateral connectivity between corresponding regions, consistent with reduced hemispheric lateralization.

entry.title: Reinforcement Learning Under Runtime Confounding: Policy Learning and Off-Policy Evaluation

link.title: Reinforcement Learning Under Runtime Confounding: Policy Learning and Off-Policy Evaluation

entry.content: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used to train robust, adaptable systems across healthcare, e-commerce, and robotics. In these settings, legal, ethical, or logistical concerns may preclude certain key variables that drive decisions from being collected during deployment time. This gives rise to a setting known as runtime confounding: the logged data hold full observability, but deployment time lacks knowledge of certain variables, known as runtime confounders. Unlike single timepoint and non-adaptive settings, runtime confounding under reinforcement learning has the potential to propagate over time, as earlier decisions affect future states, observations, and action assignments, leading to biased learning. We address these problems with three contributions: we (1) develop policy learning algorithms under runtime-confounding, (2) develop semi-parametric efficient off-policy estimation procedures, and (3) provide diagnostics for understanding the price of runtime confounding.

entry.content: A fixed spline space may limit approximation accuracy in generalized nonparametric regression with streaming data. We propose a renewable penalized-likelihood method for generalized nonparametric regression with canonical exponential-family responses. Our method combines dynamic cubic-spline refinement with Gram-metric pullback of historical score and curvature summaries. The pullback preserves the retained historical likelihood quadratic on the embedded previous spline space, while incoming data update the fit and its summaries. Under regularity and algorithmic conditions, including a growing startup and an uncapped refinement regime, we establish $L^2$-consistency at rate $O_p(N^{-2/5})$ for a fixed target in $H^2[0,1]$ and a smaller-order energy-norm discrepancy from a matched offline estimator. Simulations and applications to the Voice and Catalina datasets show that dynamic bases improve estimation when the initial representation is restrictive, with additional gains from pullback. A preliminary computational comparison also shows lower computational and storage costs than the offline methods.

entry.title: Hidden Semi-Markov Models for Fully Functional Time Series

link.title: Hidden Semi-Markov Models for Fully Functional Time Series

entry.content: Functional time series have a wide range of practical applications to modeling complex datasets such as Electroencephalogram (EEG) and other biological signals. Often latent states are hidden within the data dictating how a system is behaving and changing over time. The Hidden Markov Model (HMM) is one common and highly applicable latent state space model where the hidden state sequence evolves as a Markov chain. While the HMM has had much success modeling discrete, multivariate, and fully functional time series, it is also restricted by the Markov property which causes hidden states to persist only at geometrically decaying rates. This work investigates the implementation of hidden semi-Markov models for modeling fully functional time series data. This allows for the hidden state sequence to persist in a given state for a data-driven sojourn time, which can be parametrized by a discrete distribution (e.g. negative binomial) or left non-parametric. For efficient fitting of such a model, the hidden semi-Markov chain is embedded into a larger state space Markov chain and classic methods like the Baum-Welch and Viterbi algorithms are applied. We furthermore consider functional time series in the general setting of Gaussian measures in locally convex topological vector spaces. This is applied to a time series of pediatric EEG signals collected via overnight polysomnography.

link.title: Revisiting Generalized Median Estimators: Exact Bitwise Computation and Gray Code Acceleration

entry.content: Generalized median estimators evaluate the median of a symmetric kernel over all $M = \binom{n}{k}$ subsets of size $k$. Exhaustive evaluation was considered impractical even for $n = 29, k = 5$ ($M = 118,755$), prompting stochastic subsampling (Wilde and Grimshaw, 2013). We show that this barrier is computational, not combinatorial: storing all subsets requires $\Theta(kM)$ space, whereas stateful enumeration uses $\mathcal{O}(k)$ auxiliary state and retains only $M$ kernel values. We combine two exhaustive traversals with three-way Quickselect and a deterministic median-of-medians fallback, giving worst-case $\mathcal{O}(M)$ selection. Gosper’s successor takes $\mathcal{O}(k)$ kernel work per subset for $n < w$; a Revolving Door Gray code changes one element out and one in, enabling $\mathcal{O}(1)$ kernel updates between recalibrations and $\mathcal{O}(M + kM/P)$ total time. We derive floating-point error bounds for the location ($h_1$) and mean-centered sample variance ($h_2$) kernels and their resulting median. For $n = 29, k = 5$, our ANSI C implementation evaluates all $118,755$ subsets in $0.74$ ms and $0.71$ ms, respectively. A direct C sweep places the crossover with partial lexicographic unranking at approximately $18,000$-$23,000$ subsets ($15\%$-$19\%$ of $M$), below the $32,160$-$45,420$ subsets required by Wilde and Grimshaw’s sequential approximation at $\epsilon = 0.01$.

entry.title: Exact Online $Q_n$ Estimation: Exploiting Sliding-Window Rank Invariance

link.title: Exact Online $Q_n$ Estimation: Exploiting Sliding-Window Rank Invariance

entry.content: The $Q_n$ scale estimator (Rousseeuw and Croux, 1993) combines a 50% finite-sample breakdown point with high Gaussian efficiency, but its computation requires selecting an order statistic among the $\binom{n}{2}$ pairwise distances. We study exact online $Q_n$ computation in a sliding window by exploiting temporal rank coherence between consecutive windows. Formalizing the multiset decomposition of surviving pairwise distances in terms of strict and weak rank counts, we derive a tie-exact dual-rank update that verifies whether the previous unscaled estimate remains valid in $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$ comparisons while maintaining the sorted window in $\mathcal{O}(n)$ time. When the target rank shifts by $m$ positions, a localized row-heap procedure initialized via a monotonic two-pointer frontier scan extracts the new exact order statistic in $\mathcal{O}(n + m\log n)$ comparisons without materializing the difference matrix, complemented by a hybrid fallback that executes frontier-guided implicit matrix selection in $\mathcal{O}(n\log n)$ time for larger rank shifts. On deterministic multi-regime stress streams, our implementation matches the offline batch reference. In repeated same-platform benchmarks on a synthetic Gaussian stream, our implementation achieves median internal throughputs from 2,220,000 updates/s ($n=25$) and 1,140,000 updates/s ($n=51$) to 127,000 updates/s ($n=201$), outperforming both the exact FQN baseline ($2.5\times$ to $6.4\times$) and the approximate AFQN sketch ($1.3\times$ to $2.7\times$) across all tested window sizes.

entry.title: Estimating contextual networks via Fisher-scoring surrogate likelihood

link.title: Estimating contextual networks via Fisher-scoring surrogate likelihood

entry.content: When networks are accompanied by vertex-level covariates, effectively integrating and aligning the information underlying both data sources becomes a natural yet critical task. Current spectral approaches, despite their popularity, may yield suboptimal results and necessitate the specification of additional tuning parameters that are contingent upon unobservable signal-to-noise ratios. We propose a tuning-free, likelihood-based learning framework for estimating latent positions in contextual generalized random dot product graphs in the presence of high-dimensional vertex covariates with a low-rank structure. Our method constructs a smooth surrogate likelihood and implements a Fisher-scoring algorithm to iteratively estimate latent positions without introducing additional tuning parameters that depend on the network sparsity. We establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the Fisher-scoring estimator. Application to real-world data further demonstrates the method’s practical utility, offering a principled and scalable alternative to spectral approaches for analyzing contextual networks in high-dimensional settings.

entry.title: Estimating conditional means under missingness-not-at-random with incomplete auxiliary variables

link.title: Estimating conditional means under missingness-not-at-random with incomplete auxiliary variables

entry.content: Estimators assuming missingness at random (MAR) can fail under missingness not at random (MNAR). Introducing complete auxiliary variables sometimes restores MAR by breaking dependence between analysis variables and missingness. However, if the auxiliaries are themselves incomplete, MAR typically remains violated. We derive necessary and sufficient, weaker-than-MAR conditions under which the MAR functional $\mu_{\rm MAR}$ for a conditional mean $E[Y \mid X]$ is correct. We also propose an alternative identifying functional for $E[Y \mid X]$, called $\mu_{\rm MIA}$ for “Marginalization over Incomplete Auxiliaries”, along with sufficient conditions for $\mu_{\rm MIA}$ to be correct. For MNAR distributions in which all missingness patterns can occur and certain context-specific independences do not occur, there are two straightforward cases where $\mu_{\rm MIA}$ is correct for a strict superset of the MNAR distributions for which $\mu_{\rm MAR}$ is correct: (1) $X$ is complete and $Y$ is incomplete; or (2) all auxiliary variables are incomplete. In case (1), $\mu_{\rm MAR}$ is always incorrect, barring knife-edge cases. Determining whether either case holds requires no knowledge of the MNAR mechanism. We propose estimators of $\mu_{\rm MIA}$, including g-computation and doubly robust estimators. Our R package miapack implements a semiparametric iterated-conditional-expectations estimator. We illustrate with real data and present simulations comparing estimators of $\mu_{\rm MIA}$ and $\mu_{\rm MAR}$.

entry.title: Uncovering Multimorbidity Patterns Through a Novel Randomized Clustering Algorithm

link.title: Uncovering Multimorbidity Patterns Through a Novel Randomized Clustering Algorithm

entry.content: Patients with several chronic conditions rarely share the same combination: in four years of the nationally representative Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS), we find 32,789 distinct combinations of two to seven conditions, and over 90% of those involving four or more occur in a single patient. Methods that search for common combinations discard most of this heterogeneity. We present the Randomized Length Sequential Clustering Algorithm (RLSCA), which links diseases by lift, a pairwise association measure counted only above a user-set support threshold. A mixed-integer program repeatedly selects and removes the group of conditions with the greatest internal lift, up to a random size; 100 iterations yield a database of clusters scored by size, rediscovery frequency, and body systems spanned. In MEPS 2019, stratified by age and sex, RLSCA recovers known groupings at a high threshold, such as diabetes with lipid disorders and hypertension, and at a lower threshold returns clusters of up to eight conditions spanning five body systems. Frequent itemset mining, at its lowest feasible support, finds no set above five conditions; hierarchical clustering cannot control cluster size. With a clinical large language model, the database could suggest which further conditions a patient is at risk of.

entry.title: MG-EDA: Maturity-Gated Skew-Normal Estimation of Distribution Algorithms

link.title: MG-EDA: Maturity-Gated Skew-Normal Estimation of Distribution Algorithms

entry.content: Gaussian estimation of distribution algorithms shrink their variance on slopes and stall far from the optimum. This paper equips the corrections that act along the direction of movement – a mean shift, an elongation of the covariance along the path and a skewness – with the rule they lack: a calibrated gate, driven by a maturity statistic of the population, decides whether, how strongly and for how long each correction acts, and when the gate is closed the algorithm is exactly the estimation of multivariate normal algorithm (EMNA). The statistic is a cumulative path of whitened mean shifts with an inverse-Wishart correction, whose expectation is one under a null model without systematic movement and whose quantiles give thresholds with known false-alarm rate. It gates the three corrections as three rank-one terms of one matrix sampling equation, the skewness being carried by a skew-normal sampler that preserves the estimated mean and covariance; all vanish at maturity. We call the resulting algorithm the maturity-gated EDA (MG-EDA). A full factorial study on a training set of black-box optimization benchmarking (BBOB) functions separates the parameters: variance scaling is the prerequisite, the mean shift needs a feedback correction removing the injected shift from the statistic, the elongation turns the variance loss on a slope into a gain, and the skewness substitutes for the mean shift rather than complementing it. On held-out instances MG-EDA with the first- and second-order corrections is significantly better than the skewness-only predecessor and than EMNA with variance scaling, ties with EMNA with anticipated mean shift, and trails the adapted maximum-likelihood Gaussian model (AMaLGaM) in 20 dimensions.

entry.title: A generalized Bayesian method for identifying local and global changepoints in dynamic network data

link.title: A generalized Bayesian method for identifying local and global changepoints in dynamic network data

entry.content: We introduce a generalized Bayesian approach to multiple changepoint analysis in dynamic network data based on a multinomial log loss function and a prior distribution that imposes low-rank structure and sparsity on the model parameters. The method can detect local and global changes in network structure by incorporating information from both the full adjacency matrices and network summary statistics. Moreover, the proposed method is agnostic to the true data-generating process. From the generalized posterior distribution, we can make simultaneous inferences with meaningful uncertainty quantification about the locations of changepoints as well as deduce the network attributes and summary statistics that characterize them. For posterior simulation, we develop an efficient Gibbs sampler based on P'olya-Gamma data augmentation with a computational cost that grows linearly with the number of observed edges in the dynamic network. Simulations across several benchmark network models show that the proposed method is often more accurate and flexible than competitors. We demonstrate the practical value of the method through applications to an email communication network and an international conflict network.

entry.title: Subspace Inference for Multilayer Latent Space Networks: Intrinsic Geometry and One-Step Estimator

link.title: Subspace Inference for Multilayer Latent Space Networks: Intrinsic Geometry and One-Step Estimator

entry.content: Multilayer networks on a common node set, such as brain connectomes of several animals with one layer per animal, often share a low-dimensional geometry but differ in how strongly each layer expresses it and in node activity. We study a multilayer latent space network model that combines an invariant subspace common to all layers with layer-specific interaction matrices and node-by-layer degree effects. By introducing the generalized Cayley transform of the invariant subspace, we characterize the intrinsic geometry of the model and obtain sharp convergence rates for the maximum likelihood estimator, asymptotic normality and Neyman orthogonality for vertex-level parameters, and asymptotic normality for the interaction matrices with a non-negligible bias. Plug-in estimates of the bias and covariance give debiased confidence regions and tests of equality between layers. We also propose an easy-to-implement one-step estimator that attains the same vertex-level limits. In a real-world mouse connectome dataset, the inbred strain that lacks a corpus callosum shows about twice the hemispheric segregation of the other three strains.

entry.title: Beware of complexity bias: A hindrance to conceptual model generalization and interpretability

link.title: Beware of complexity bias: A hindrance to conceptual model generalization and interpretability

entry.content: In the field of rainfall-runoff modeling, lumped conceptual models have been shown to be powerful representations of catchment filtering functions. They demonstrate fairly strong predictive performance in gauged catchments and have the ability to learn important intermediate latent variables and flow paths which increases their value as interpretable models. During calibration, these conceptual models may fit streamflow just as well as deep learning models, however, their performance often sharply degrades after deployment, suggesting the presence of overfitting. We hypothesize that complexity (or flexibility) bias is one of the causes of such overfitting. Complexity bias can appear within conceptual models when the number of effective degrees of freedom is parameter or flow path dependent. Using a popular conceptual model and a series of synthetic datasets, we illustrate the presence of complexity bias and demonstrate its impact on model interpretability/parameter inference. Then, using real rainfall-runoff data from CAMELS-US, we investigate if overfitting can be reduced by adding regularization terms that prevent complexity bias from forming. Our results suggest that conceptual and hybrid modeling can be further improved if hydrologists become aware of this pervasive bias.

entry.title: graphMTP: An R Shiny Interface for Graphical Multiple Testing and Interim Monitoring

link.title: graphMTP: An R Shiny Interface for Graphical Multiple Testing and Interim Monitoring

entry.content: Graphical multiple testing procedures provide a framework for controlling the family-wise error rate across endpoints, treatment comparisons, and patient populations in confirmatory clinical trials. Interim monitoring requires analysts to track changing local significance levels together with hypothesis-specific testing schedules. We present graphMTP, an R application built with shiny, for constructing hypothesis graphs, specifying per-hypothesis group-sequential plans, and inspecting alpha recycling. The application uses TrialSimulator for graph updates, gsDesign for spending profiles, and rpact for boundary calculations. It records the local levels, boundaries, and decisions used for each submitted test and exports designs and histories as JSON files. Worked examples cover fixed-design reallocation, fixed-sequence gatekeeping, delayed activation, and retesting a previously monitored recipient of alpha. Replication code checks graph updates, normal crossing probabilities, and saved-session replay. Sequential tests use a prespecified information schedule and reconstruct the complete local boundary family at the current allocation, including after recycling. Historical event records retain the boundaries actually used. An installable package and standalone sources accompany the article.

entry.title: What Does Matching a Human Intervention Effect Establish? Benchmark Checks for LLM Simulations

link.title: What Does Matching a Human Intervention Effect Establish? Benchmark Checks for LLM Simulations

entry.content: LLM simulations are validated by equivalence with human effects, yet a zero reference passes whenever the human 90 percent interval lies inside the margin, as the human benchmark shows before simulation. When the zero reference fails, planned precision gives independent simulations the margin up to which passing is a 5 percent test of response. In an exploratory 70-experiment reanalysis, 72 percent of GPT-4’s $\pm$0.20 SD passes were zero-reference passes; GPT-4 passed 16 contrasts the zero reference failed (1.58 expected without response). In a preregistered audit, Claude Sonnet 5.5 passed three intention targets, all zero-reference passes, and the registered belief-gradient control; norm beliefs changed 0.065 SD against humans’ 0.351 (zero-reference check added after unblinding; norm beliefs emphasized after inspection). Registered tests detected no overestimation; average-effect intervals excluded overestimation above 0.08 SD. A group audit’s precision floor is 1.33 facts against a 2.9-fact effect. Report the zero-reference threshold beside every equivalence decision.

entry.title: Parareal Approximation of Stochastic $L^2$-Boosting

link.title: Parareal Approximation of Stochastic $L^2$-Boosting

entry.content: We study Parareal approximations of stochastic (L^2)-boosting, reusing the learner draws of the sequential algorithm in the fine propagators. We establish mean-square error bounds whose order improves with each correction, characterize the limiting distributions of normalized errors, including non-Gaussian components and the effects of coarse discretization, and derive sufficient conditions for preserving the statistical limit laws and validation-based stopping behavior of the sequential algorithm. Numerical experiments with sample-dependent coordinate and nonlinear residual-fitting learners examine the predicted convergence rates and limiting distributions, while computational benchmarks assess the efficiency of the method relative to sequential implementations.

entry.title: MSRyzen: An Agentic Platform for Unified Proteomics Analysis and Evidence-Centric Visualization

link.title: MSRyzen: An Agentic Platform for Unified Proteomics Analysis and Evidence-Centric Visualization

entry.content: Mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics is essential for comprehensive protein characterization, yet it relies on multistep computational workflows that typically demand tedious manual parameter tuning and complex software integration. Here, we present MSRyzen, an agent-driven framework that provides automated parameter optimization and extensible tool integration across bottom-up and top-down proteomics workflows. MSRyzen translates natural-language prompts into directed acyclic workflow graphs, optimizes analytical parameters guided by quantitative metrics and user-defined objectives, and incorporates new third-party software through standardized callable interfaces. Across four public top-down datasets, automated parameter optimization increased proteoform identifications by 3.6% to 15.8% compared to default settings at a 1% false discovery rate. To ensure transparent data interpretation, an interactive visualization interface coordinates identification metrics with peak-level spectral evidence and sequence coverage. Integrating adaptive tuning with multi-tiered spectral inspection, MSRyzen delivers an end-to-end, fully automated framework, dramatically reducing the operational barrier to modern mass spectrometry data analysis.

entry.title: Smoothed Conformal Testing with Small Calibration Sets

link.title: Smoothed Conformal Testing with Small Calibration Sets

entry.content: A small calibration sample restricts split conformal $p$-values to a coarse rank grid. Randomization removes this discretization, but its effect depends on both the smoothing interval and the allocation of auxiliary random variables. Independent tie-block randomization is exactly valid under null exchangeability. When calibration and null scores are jointly exchangeable conditional on the alternative scores, we prove positive regression dependence and hence Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate control, including for atomic score distributions. Smoothing over calibration-dependent rank cells agrees with tie-block randomization when calibration scores are distinct and no test score ties a calibration score, but can fail marginal validity with atoms. Assigning sorted random draws according to score order can invalidate even a single null $p$-value. entry.title: Combining Past Experimental Data for Efficient Estimation: A Shrinkage Approach

link.title: Combining Past Experimental Data for Efficient Estimation: A Shrinkage Approach

We also provide managerial guidance on which shrinkage estimator to use based on average bias and bias dispersion.

entry.title: Deep conditional distribution estimation via nonparametric exponential tilt models

link.title: Deep conditional distribution estimation via nonparametric exponential tilt models

entry.content: Estimating the conditional distribution of a response $Y$ given covariates $X$ is a fundamental problem in statistics, underlying prediction, feature estimation, and dependence assessment. We propose a unified nonparametric representation of the conditional density, a nonparametric exponential tilt model, in which the dependence between $Y$ and $X$ is captured by an interaction function $\phi(x,y)$ while both baseline densities are left unspecified. We establish identifiability and develop a nonparametric likelihood method that profiles out the baselines by empirical likelihood, with non-asymptotic error bounds under general sieve conditions. Because the profile likelihood admits no closed-form or readily tractable population counterpart, standard empirical process arguments do not apply; we therefore establish a new exponential tail bound for the supremum of a canonical U-process under a uniform entropy condition, a result we show to be new to the U-process literature and of independent interest, with a largely self-contained proof. The framework unifies several inferential tasks: mutual density ratio and mutual information estimation; a general theory for conditional features, including means, quantiles and distribution functions, without separate smoothness assumptions on the individual conditional feature functions; and a finite-sample valid permutation test of independence. Under deep neural network sieves, the convergence rates depend on the intrinsic complexity of $\phi$ rather than the ambient dimension. Simulations demonstrate that the proposed method attains uniformly smaller estimation errors than existing conditional density and mutual density-ratio estimators, and delivers markedly higher power in independence testing when dependence is oscillatory or high-dimensional, while remaining comparable to established tests in standard settings.

entry.title: Statistical and Machine Learning Approaches for Estimating Visitation to Natural Spaces in the UK

link.title: Statistical and Machine Learning Approaches for Estimating Visitation to Natural Spaces in the UK

entry.content: Natural spaces support health and well-being, but increasing recreational use can put pressure on ecologically sensitive sites. Understanding when, where and why people visit is important for planning, site management and evaluating interventions. Building on work by the Office for National Statistics, we developed statistical and machine learning models to predict visitor numbers at points located in natural spaces. We trained on automated people counter data across a range of green and blue spaces in England and Wales and tested the models’ ability to generalise to unseen counter locations. Our models offer a scalable approach for predicting visitor numbers in natural spaces, reducing reliance on surveys and physical counters.

entry.title: Efficient inference for fairness-constrained sequential decision policies

link.title: Efficient inference for fairness-constrained sequential decision policies

entry.content: Adaptive decision systems in education and health choose interventions sequentially and are often required not to leave a protected group too far behind. We study the fairness-constrained optimal value: the largest population value attainable by a policy in a smooth parametric class subject to constraints that are smooth functions of group specific counterfactual functionals, such as value gaps, floors, max-min welfare and budgets. For multi-stage, non-Markov data under sequential ignorability, a sensitivity analysis of the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker system shows that this value is pathwise differentiable, with efficient influence function equal to the Lagrangian combination of the influence functions of the group values. The same analysis gives the influence functions of the optimal policy, the multiplier and the group values it delivers. A cross-fitted doubly robust estimator is efficient despite its data-dependent feasible set and yields confidence intervals for the constrained value and the price of fairness. When the constraint binds, any plug-in fair policy violates the population constraint, by a margin that vanishes as the sample grows, with probability tending to one half; tightening the estimated constraint by a one sided confidence margin certifies fairness at a small cost in value. Exact checks, simulations and a synthetic case study illustrate the theory.

entry.title: Synthetic Surrogate Functional Regression (SSFR): A Robust Framework for Estimating Spatially Varying Covariate Effects in Surrogate-Augmented Neuroimaging

link.title: Synthetic Surrogate Functional Regression (SSFR): A Robust Framework for Estimating Spatially Varying Covariate Effects in Surrogate-Augmented Neuroimaging

entry.content: Relating demographic, clinical, and genetic covariates to high-dimensional imaging outcomes is a core problem in brain imaging, especially when the target modality is observed for only a subset of participants. Generative models can synthesize missing modalities from auxiliary data, but using synthetic images in regression requires care to ensure valid inference. We propose a two-stage Synthetic Surrogate Functional Regression (SSFR) framework for spatially varying covariate effects under partially observed imaging outcomes. By calibrating surrogate information against observed target images, SSFR improves efficiency while remaining robust to discrepancies between the surrogate and target regression functions. We establish consistency and the convergence rate of the estimator, and show that first-stage surrogate-model estimation error does not alter its asymptotic rate. We introduce a voxelwise surrogate explanatory measure $R^2(z)$, the fraction of residual target-image variation explained by a candidate surrogate; with the observation rate, it gives a principled criterion for surrogate screening and indicates the potential efficiency gain. We further develop a weighted bootstrap procedure for simultaneous confidence corridors (SCCs). As surrogate informativeness increases, SCC widths approach those obtained under complete observation, improving localization of significant effects that cannot be identified from the observed data alone. Simulations confirm accuracy and robustness under surrogate misspecification and with surrogates generated by image-to-image neural networks. Applied to spatially normalized PET images from ADNI, SSFR yields interpretable coefficient maps and uniformly narrower SCCs than an analysis using observed PET alone, enlarging the region over which age-related metabolic decline is simultaneously significant.

entry.title: Energy-preserving Bayesian model reduction: closed-form structured posteriors and probabilistic stability certificates for quadratic operator inference

link.title: Energy-preserving Bayesian model reduction: closed-form structured posteriors and probabilistic stability certificates for quadratic operator inference

entry.content: Bayesian operator inference learns reduced-order models (ROMs) with polynomial structure from state data and returns a closed-form Gaussian posterior over the reduced operators. That posterior is unconstrained, so it gives positive probability to operators with unbounded dynamics, and current practice controls this only through finite-horizon simulation tests on a few samples. We show that energy preservation of the quadratic operator is a set of linear equality constraints, which can be imposed exactly inside the Bayesian formulation without losing the closed form. In particular, the constrained posterior follows from one Kalman-type update of the unconstrained one, and its samples are obtained exactly, by the same correction applied to unconstrained draws. Under this structure, global boundedness for all initial conditions and bounded inputs reduces to a linear matrix condition on the symmetric part of the linear operator. The simulation test is then replaced by a probabilistic stability certificate: the posterior probability that the ROM is globally bounded, estimated with exact confidence bounds; the posterior restricted to certified models is then sampled exactly by rejection. For energy-conserving systems, the linear part can be constrained to be skew-symmetric as well: every draw then grows at most linearly in time, and conserves energy exactly when unforced. On a forced viscous Burgers’ equation, the Korteweg-de Vries equation and a two-dimensional viscous Burgers’ equation, every sample of the constrained posterior integrates to a bounded trajectory, where up to all unconstrained draws diverge, and beyond the observation window the former is also the more accurate of the two.

entry.title: Scalable Matrix-Free Algorithms for Variance Estimation of Survey-Weighted Survival Curves

link.title: Scalable Matrix-Free Algorithms for Variance Estimation of Survey-Weighted Survival Curves

entry.content: Variance estimation for survey-weighted survival curves using existing statistical software can require substantial time and memory, particularly when the number of distinct event times is large. We developed two matrix-free algorithms that compute the conventional Taylor linearization variance estimator without constructing the full event-time covariance matrix: one accumulates individual-level linearization contributions, while the other directly updates aggregated contributions at the primary sampling unit (PSU) level. We evaluated numerical accuracy, runtime, and peak memory usage through an application to the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS) and simulation experiments. Both approaches yielded survival and variance estimates identical to the R implementation. In the 7-year follow-up analysis of 7,608 NHATS participants with 2,879 deaths, computation time decreased from approximately 26 minutes to less than 3 seconds with the individual-level approach and less than 1 second with the PSU-level approach. Simulations with sample sizes of 1,000 to 10,000 showed similar results, with more pronounced computational advantages as sample size and the number of distinct event times increased. In more demanding settings, the existing implementation failed due to memory exhaustion, whereas both proposed approaches completed successfully. Matrix-free computation can improve the efficiency and scalability of design-based variance estimation while preserving numerical accuracy.

entry.title: The Science and Mythology of Sports Rankings: Evaluating the methods, assumptions, and attributes used to rank NCAA teams

link.title: The Science and Mythology of Sports Rankings: Evaluating the methods, assumptions, and attributes used to rank NCAA teams

entry.content: Selecting a sports-ranking system is not a purely mathematical decision. It also requires agreement about what the ranking should mean and what institutional purpose it should serve. This paper distinguishes four related but different tasks in sports ranking: prediction, retrospective evaluation, championship selection, and seeding; compares the governing philosophies of major ranking families; and identifies recurring errors in ranking debates. A descriptive comparison of nine NCAA Division I sport settings illustrates how schedule density, scoring environment, cross-conference connectivity, head-to-head meetings, and common-opponent availability vary from sport to sport. The central premise is that no ranking methodology is value-free. Every system reflects choices about evidence, competitive merit, and which tradeoffs are acceptable. The paper therefore offers a structured, multi-objective framework for evaluating ranking systems according to their intended purpose/goal rather than naming one universally superior method. Its principal contribution is to make the philosophical and institutional assumptions behind ranking decisions explicit, comparable, and testable.

entry.title: Multi-scale dynamic latent space models improve inference for a social predator

link.title: Multi-scale dynamic latent space models improve inference for a social predator

entry.content: Social networks are dynamic in nature. Examining changes in dynamic networks provides insights into the drivers and consequences of social interactions. Dynamic latent space models (DLSMs) quantify social tie strength through a distance measure between latent positions in an unobservable, low-dimensional space. Conditional on the latent positions, ties are assumed independent, and temporal dynamics are introduced through autocorrelated trajectories. These trajectories are typically modeled as random walks; however, random walks lack the mechanism to characterize network clustering, where individuals from the same group tend to form stronger ties than those across groups. Therefore, we extend the framework of DLSM to distinguish within-group dynamics from between-group dynamics. Our approach employs coupled movement models operating at two scales in the latent space to encode community structure using autoregressive processes with attraction. Through simulation studies, we show that when cluster separation is high, our framework improves coverage of linear predictors and enhances overall model fit relative to a naive DLSM. When cluster separation is moderate, performance remains comparable to that of the naive approach. In addition, our method demonstrates empirical computational advantages over the naive DLSM, with potential for further efficiency gains. We apply our framework to a case study of gray wolf (Canis lupus) interactions over three decades in Yellowstone National Park, where it provides improved model performance and novel insights into wolf social dynamics.

entry.title: Extreme Value Inference with Measurement Error: Application to Earthquake Magnitudes

link.title: Extreme Value Inference with Measurement Error: Application to Earthquake Magnitudes

entry.content: Extreme value analyses typically assume that observations are measured without error, yet many environmental measurements are subject to different levels of observational uncertainty depending on the context. Ignoring such measurement error can distort inference on the tail behaviour. In this paper, we focus on peaks-over-threshold models, where exceedances above a high threshold are typically modelled using the generalised Pareto distribution (GPD). We develop a statistical framework for extreme value inference when observations are noisy measurements of an underlying true variable. Measurement error introduces a particular challenge in threshold-based extreme value analysis, as latent exceedances may be observed below the threshold, while latent non-exceedances may be observed above it. To address this problem, we represent the latent distribution using a hybrid body–tail specification, combining a flexible nonparametric body with a GPD tail. We develop a computationally efficient partially censored likelihood inference approach for data of this structure. The framework allows the measurement error scale and the GPD parameters to depend on covariates. Simulation studies demonstrate biases on the tail inference from ignoring measurement error and that our approach overcomes such impacts. The methodology is motivated by, and illustrated using, the catalogue of induced earthquake magnitudes from the Groningen, Netherlands, one of the largest gas fields in the world.

entry.title: The Fiscal and Economic Implications of Green Mandates: a Boltzmann Approach to Public Governance

link.title: The Fiscal and Economic Implications of Green Mandates: a Boltzmann Approach to Public Governance

entry.content: Public authorities increasingly need to translate multifaceted policy objectives into concrete fiscal and investment choices while accounting for their socioeconomic consequences. A credible ex-ante impact assessment should report downstream implications attributable to the historical baseline and specified policy targets, without introducing discretionary assumptions about unknown administrative, socioeconomic or other physical processes. Bringing the large-scale perspective of statistical physics to public governance, we construct such an ex-ante impact assessment. Its scope encompasses policy objectives that condition a finite number of generalized moments of observables in the historical baseline, which comprises a sufficiently large collection of projects or public programmes. As a proof-of-principle application, we consider the green transition in the energy-generation sector using the historical baseline of many infrastructure projects from the World Bank. Our earlier results deriving closed-form expressions for coarse-grained combinatorial probabilities enable a tractable statistical and downstream assessment. We assess the statistical compatibility of the historical baseline with different levels of green-power surplus and demonstrate how the same statistical-physics construction can estimate any downstream metric expressible through arbitrary functions of generalized moments of the baseline observables. In the absence of more detailed knowledge about the processes forming the historical baseline, large-scale universality, whenever many unknown influences on collective phenomena become negligible, unambiguously offers a principled route to a self-contained ex-ante impact assessment.
